claims.text: The untreated alloy is equal-atomic NbMoTaW.
Untreated equal-atomic NbMoTaW has a single-phase BCC structure.
Untreated NbMoTaW has excellent mechanical performance at 1600 °C.
Untreated NbMoTaW has very poor room-temperature ductility.
The irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW has been proposed through first-principles calculations.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 5 at% Zr to NbMoTaW.
Approximately 5 at% Zr will increase the room-temperature tensile ductility of NbMoTaW.
Zr will segregate modestly to NbMoTaW grain boundaries.
Zr addition may produce nanoscale solid-solution fluctuations in NbMoTaW.
Zr segregation or nanoscale chemical fluctuations will enhance grain-boundary cohesion.
Zr segregation or nanoscale chemical fluctuations will lower barriers to dislocation nucleation and motion.
Zr locally modifies grain-boundary chemistry and reduces dislocation pinning, thereby relieving room-temperature brittleness.
A minor Zr addition around 5 at% will preserve the overall BCC phase.
The Zr-modified alloy will retain mechanical performance at 1600 °C comparable to untreated NbMoTaW.
The Zr-modified alloy will retain irradiation resistance at least comparable to untreated NbMoTaW.
The high-temperature mechanics and irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW rely on phase stability and defect-recombination mechanisms.
The ductility benefit is expected only over a limited range of minor Zr additions around 5 at%.
Excessive Zr may cause secondary-phase formation or excessive segregation.
Secondary-phase formation or excessive Zr segregation could compromise high-temperature properties or irradiation resistance.

contradictions.description: The material-initial-state field says irradiation resistance has only been proposed by first-principles calculations, whereas the baseline field presents the untreated alloy as possessing irradiation resistance without retaining that qualification.
